value.text: Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday as rain moves into the area, with heavier rainfall possible in the evening. The district said it made the decision as a precaution based on information from the National Weather Service . Parents and guardians are encouraged to consider conditions in their neighborhoods. Absences caused by weather will be excused, the district said. Heavier rain is possible Wednesday through Friday and could lead to school closures. The district is monitoring conditions with the St. Lucie County Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district said it will announce any changes to Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics based on weather conditions. Families should check the district’s official channels for updates. Neighboring Indian River County schools will also operate on a modified schedule Tuesday, Nov. 17, with students dismissed early, according to the School District of Indian River County. The district announced the following dismissal times: High schools: 12:20 p.m. Middle schools and K-8: 1 p.m. Elementary schools: 1:50 p.m. Wabasso School: 12:30 p.m. Morning arrival times will remain unchanged, and transportation will operate as normal during early dismissal. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but closed in the afternoon. All extracurricular activities must conclude by 2:30 p.m. The district said additional updates will be shared as information becomes available. RELATED: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across south Florida Palm Beach County schools are still scheduled to open Tuesday, Nov. The district will continue monitoring the weather and share updates if anything changes. Okeechobee County schools will also be open. Martin County schools will also remain open Tuesday; however, all after-school activities will be cancelled. The ground is already soaked from the rain we experienced the first weekend of the month, so it won't take much to create flooding concerns. Right now, up to 4-5 inches of rain is possible, but higher isolated amounts can't be ruled out.

Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

A major crash blocked two left lanes on southbound I-95 in Martin County beyond Exit 96 for Hobe Sound on Monday morning, according to the Florida Department of Transportation’s FL511 traffic system. The crash was reported at about 11:15 a.m. and was still affecting traffic as of 11:21 a.m. Drivers should expect delays and use caution approaching the area. A second crash nearby has also impacted traffic in the northbound lanes. According to the Florida Highway Patrol, one crash involves a single vehicle, and the second involves three vehicles. No injuries have been reported in either crash. All vehicles have been moved off the roadway. Traffic congestion remains due to the incidents; however, traffic flow is expected to improve shortly. No further details about the crash or any injuries were immediately available. Check FL511 for the latest traffic updates. for the latest traffic updates.

Hundreds of Riviera Beach residents packed an emergency City Council meeting seeking financial assistance after November flooding damaged homes, displaced families and left residents questioning how they will pay for repairs.The city discussed setting aside $2 million for a proposed forgivable loan or grant program for residents whose homes were damaged by the flooding. The proposed assistance would help pay for interior and exterior repairs needed to make homes safe and livable.But during the heated meeting, city Finance Director Randy Sherman said the city faces restrictions on using public money to pay for damage to private property, creating uncertainty about how the proposed relief could move forward.Weeks after floodwaters inundated homes in Lone Pine Estates, residents filled the meeting room, with others standing outside, hoping city leaders would provide a path toward recovery.Keisha Harty’s lives in the neighborhood and her home was impacted by the flooding. She summed up the growing frustration in the neighborhood.“No help is coming. We are on our own,” said Harty.Another resident challenged the city's position that public funding could not be used directly to help private homeowners, pointing to other causes the city has supported.“When you say you can’t use federal dollars or public funding for private citizens, I have to disagree,” the resident said. “I’m looking for a Lone Pine relief fundraiser.”Council member Shirley Lanier argued the flooding and its impact on residents should be treated as a broader public safety concern.“That is a public safety issue,” Lanier said. “There is no way that we cannot use public money for a public concern.”Residents also used the meeting to show city leaders what recovery has looked like on the ground.One woman said firefighters rescued her from floodwaters. At the podium, she displayed basic items she said she received afterward, including a T-shirt, deodorant and socks.“Why is this being given to a taxpayer on an emergency event?” she asked.The frustrations come as families continue trying to clean up and repair homes weeks after the flooding.Many residents are also concerned about additional rainfall and the possibility that already hard-hit neighborhoods could face more flooding.The Riviera Beach City Council unanimously voted to amend a motion to continue considering the $2 million emergency set-aside while seeking a legal opinion on how the money could be used.The proposal calls for establishing a forgivable loan or grant program specifically for residents whose homes were damaged by the November flooding.City leaders also considered partnerships that could provide emergency shelter, hotel or motel vouchers and temporary housing for displaced residents.Another proposal would allow the city to coordinate mutual aid with neighboring cities, counties and partner agencies for debris removal, collection and other flood recovery needs.The vote does not mean homeowners will immediately receive money. Instead, it keeps the proposed assistance moving forward as city officials examine the legal options available for providing relief.A representative from U.S. Lois Frankel’s office told residents that the office was working with federal and state officials to seek disaster assistance. According to the representative, a letter related to the effort was awaiting President Donald Trump’s signature.For residents who have already spent weeks dealing with flood damage, however, uncertainty over when additional help could arrive remains a major concern.“They’re not gonna help us, and if they do it will be a miracle,” said Harty.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Flight cancellations are dropping as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop, but passengers are still dealing with delays, long layovers and an important question: What does an airline owe you when your flight is canceled?WATCH: Samantha Gutierrez's report for what passengers need to knowFederal passenger protections provide a clear right in one key situation. If an airline cancels your flight and you decide not to travel, you are entitled to a refund, regardless of what caused the cancellation. That includes nonrefundable tickets. Hotels, meals and ground transportation are a different story. Because Friday's disruption originated with the FAA rather than an airline, carriers are not universally required to cover those additional expenses, though individual airlines may voluntarily provide assistance.At President Donald J. Trump International Airport, passenger Scott Danforth said the disruption left him frustrated by what he sees as an imbalance between the responsibilities of travelers and airlines."If we make cancellations, we get to pay a lot of money," Danforth told WPTV. "But they can make cancellations, and there's no consequence. That's what I don't like."Paul Hudson of FlyersRights.org said passengers whose flights are canceled have an important decision to make."You can choose the offer of rebooking, or you can get a refund," Hudson said.Under U.S. Department of Transportation rules, passengers do not have to accept airline credits or travel vouchers in place of a refund when the airline cancels their flight and they decide not to travel. Another family WPTV met at the airport said their journey home now includes a 13-hour layover."Maybe they could give us, like, a hotel or something through all this chaos," traveler Jessica Soros said.Hudson said passengers should ask their airline what assistance is available, but accommodations such as meals, hotel rooms and ground transportation aren't guaranteed when the disruption is outside the carrier's control."They may provide it to some passengers ... but they don't have to," Hudson said.Travelers should still ask their carrier about meal vouchers, hotel assistance, discounted hotel rates and travel waivers.Travel insurance or benefits included with some credit cards may offer another option for qualifying expenses."If you have flight insurance, that should cover these kinds of things," Hudson said.Travelers should check the terms of their specific policy or credit card because coverage and reimbursement requirements vary.Flight operations were moving closer to normal Monday, though lingering cancellations and delays remained.More than 400 U.S. flights were canceled Monday and more than 18,000 were delayed, according to FlightAware figures. The continued disruption stems partly from aircraft and flight crews being left out of position following the nationwide stoppage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it takes time for airlines to move crews and planes back where they need to be.The FAA has said faulty equipment led to Friday's ground stop, while officials continue investigating the precise cause. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials had found no evidence of anything nefarious.A preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working at a remote FAA site to replace copper wiring with fiber and replace a router when the router began flooding other routers with data, according to Duffy. The exact cause remains under investigation.U.S. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., said the disruption underscores the importance of ensuring the nation's aviation system remains reliable."We need to take whatever steps we can to make sure people are always safe and on time," Frankel said.While the cancellation numbers are improving, travel disruptions on this scale can take time to fully work through an airline network.For anyone still affected, the key is knowing the distinction: You may be entitled to your money back if the airline canceled your flight and you choose not to travel, but additional expenses such as meals and hotels depend on the circumstances and the airline's policies. West Palm Beach residents are being urged to prepare for another round of heavy rain and possible flooding this week while parts of the city are still recovering from historic rainfall earlier this month.The city said Monday that heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding are possible from Tuesday through Thursday. According to information provided by the city from the National Weather Service, there is a 40% to 60% chance that 2 to 4 inches of rain could fall across much of South Florida's east coast, with significantly higher amounts possible in isolated locations.Additional rain could worsen flooding in areas where the ground remains saturated from the Nov. 1-2 flooding, particularly in low-lying neighborhoods.Mayor Keith James has extended West Palm Beach's local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. City officials said the extension allows West Palm Beach to continue emergency measures, coordinate resources and assist residents affected by the flooding.City crews and emergency personnel are continuing recovery work while preparing for the possibility of more flooding.According to the city, crews are monitoring affected neighborhoods and inspecting and clearing city-maintained storm drain grates.Officials are also evaluating whether garbage, recycling and yard waste collection can be accelerated in western communities hit hardest by the recent flooding to reduce the risk of additional service disruptions.The city is continuing to operate an auxiliary pumping station to lower water levels in the Apoxee Reserve. Water-control structures at Grassy Waters are also being managed to increase available storage capacity ahead of additional rainfall.City staff are meeting daily with regional partners to monitor water levels, review pumping operations and assess the capacity of the drainage system.West Palm Beach officials are asking residents to prepare now in case flooding makes travel difficult.Residents should:Monitor weather forecasts and official city updates.Avoid driving or walking through flooded areas.Use caution around standing water and storm drains.Stock up on drinking water, nonperishable food and necessary medications.Make sure they have baby supplies, pet food and other household essentials they may need if travel becomes difficult.Drivers should never attempt to travel through a flooded roadway. Water can be deeper than it appears, and flooding can hide damaged or washed-out pavement.Who residents should contact depends on where the flooding occurs:City-maintained public roads: Call the City of West Palm Beach at 561-822-2210.Communities west of Florida's Turnpike and north of Okeechobee Road: Contact the Hamal Community Development District at 561-571-0010 or oteroj@whhassociates.com.Other communities in northern and western West Palm Beach: Contact the Northern Palm Beach County Improvement District at 561-624-7830. Residents can also check the NPBCID Units of Development page to determine whether their neighborhood is within the district.Emergencies: Call 911.Residents affected by the earlier flooding can also get assistance through the Florida Division of Emergency Management's Multi-Agency Resource Center in Riviera Beach.The center brings together state and local agencies and nonprofit organizations to connect residents with recovery services and other resources.Multi-Agency Resource CenterWells Recreation Center2409 Avenue H WestRiviera Beach, FL 33404Hours: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.Additional flood recovery information is available through the Florida Division of Emergency Management.West Palm Beach officials said they will continue monitoring conditions and coordinating with emergency management agencies throughout the week.Residents can find the latest updates on the city's website.

The chance of heavy rain this week is lingering over our five-county viewing area — days after some communities in West Palm Beach dried out from a major flood event.The Hamilton Bay neighborhood in West Palm Beach was underwater last Monday, a full week after record-breaking rainfall came down. With more heavy rain in the forecast this week, neighbors tell me they're concerned.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Late Monday morning, Ashley Debrowski was out strolling the sidewalks of Hamilton Bay with her children. "A week ago today, I would still be trapped in my house," Debrowski said.Around the corner, Tushar Bulsara was in his driveway wrapping a vehicle. "That whole week was just unbelievable. It almost felt like a dream," Bulsara said.Neighbors told me their community off of Jog Road was underwater for 11 days."Eleven days of essentially being afraid to leave the house," Debrowski said."Vehicles have to be able to come in for me to do my work," Bulsara said. "And you know, that's business lost."The severe, prolonged flooding impacted communities in the Hamal Community Development District, a roughly 250-acre area near Jog Road and Florida's Turnpike that includes Hamilton Bay, Briar Bay and other neighborhoods."It's a situation that we never thought was going to happen," said Dwayne Barrett, the operations manager for the Hamal CDD.Barrett tells me that since then, the CDD has been working with other government entities to make sure that doesn't happen again."I think we're in a bigger and better place right now with additional larger pumps to what we already have already, and so that's going to help a lot to move water. It's currently in operation," Barrett said.As those extra pumps moved water out of nearby lakes and into a canal by the turnpike, the streets in Hamilton Bay are dry. But the neighbors' minds are still flooded with worry.When I asked Bulsara if he was keeping his eye on the forecast this week, he said, "Yes.""If that happens again, you know, it disrupts work, it disrupts kids going to school," Bulsara said."I will say the lake behind my house definitely looks lower today, but it still makes me really nervous because you don't want to be trapped in your house. Definitely not the way you want to live," Debrowski said.A spokeswoman for the City of West Palm Beach told me in an email that city officials are "meeting daily with regional partners to review pumping operations, monitor local water levels, and assess system capacity to ensure resources are in place to respond as conditions warrant."The city is also extending the local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 22.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Martin County has put an upcoming class of about 25 firefighters on hold while it figures out how Amendment 3 will affect its budget. Firefighters say Martin County Fire Rescue is already short-staffed and can’t afford to wait. County Administrator Don Donaldson decided after voters approved Amendment 3 on Nov. The amendment expands the homestead property tax exemption. Donaldson says it will cut the county’s property tax budgets by about 12% next year and then again the year after. I also don’t want to have a situation where we just hired somebody and then six months later have to eliminate that position or let them go, Donaldson said. Donaldson confirmed Fire Rescue has 17 vacancies right now. He said that could reach about 25 by January as employees take the county’s voluntary separation program. The union came up with the same estimate. Donaldson also said calls are up more than 10% this year. Evan Brown is a firefighter paramedic and a union representative with Local 2959. He said the department is already feeling the shortage. We already have positions that are browned out, meaning we don’t have personnel, and trucks are sitting at stations, Brown said. This is only going to make it worse. See also: Travelers still stranded at DJT airport days after nationwide ground stop Brown said fewer crews means slower response times, more overtime, and more burnout. He also said neighboring departments are hiring right now and offering better pay. He said the union had been promised Fire Rescue would keep hiring no matter what happened with Amendment 3. We spoke with the county administrator, who promised us no matter what happened with Amendment 3, we’d be hiring, Brown said. Donaldson said residents will still get the same quality of service, even if that means more overtime or changes to truck staffing. He said Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli agreed to pause the class. Donaldson plans to hold workshops with commissioners on Amendment 3. He said he hopes to have clear direction by January on how many firefighter positions the county can advertise. We need to hire, and we need the help, Brown said. We need to continue this level of service that our residents expect and deserve.

Military Trail has reopened, and the crater left behind by the deadly Learjet crash has been filled, but for families who lived just feet from where the plane came down, the road to recovery is far from over.Mariano Garcia, an attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley, is representing four families from the Greenacres mobile home community whose homes, vehicles and other property were damaged by crash debris.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," Garcia said.Those financial concerns have been a part of the aftermath since the first days following the crash.For the four families Garcia represents, the focus is now turning to financial relief for their specific losses.One of those families is a household of eight living in a mobile home roughly 50 feet from the impact site. Garcia said seven members of the family were home when the crash happened, including three who were outside."Dad was on the porch holding his 1-year-old child. Mom was standing nearby when a chunk of sidewalk came busting through their porch, narrowly missing them," Garcia said.Other members of the family were inside."They all felt the explosion, the shock. They breathed all of the residue that was in the air," Garcia said. "It was a very traumatic event for them, as you can imagine."The damage to the family's home was significant."You had chunks of aircraft parts busting through the roofs, you know, allowing the water intrusion into these residences, and when you combine that with the power being out, food spoiling in refrigerators, folks being unable to return to their homes, it had a pretty significant impact on their lives," Garcia said.Power and water have since been restored to the mobile home community, according to Garcia, but the family of eight has not been able to return to its home because the residence remains unsafe. He said the family has been staying in Airbnbs provided through charity.Garcia said there is no lawsuit at this point.Instead, he is communicating with attorneys for Aurora Aviation Inc., which does business as Upper Jets and operated the Learjet, and the company's insurance carrier in an effort to secure immediate financial relief for the four families he represents.When WPTV asked whether the company has been cooperating, Garcia's response was direct."Very much so," he said. "I'm encouraged that at least the company for this charter operator, the insurance company, is responding and acknowledging that there were losses and are doing what they can to advance sums to these families and help them out."An inspector is expected to assess the affected properties as Garcia's team works to determine the extent of the losses.For now, Garcia said the immediate focus is on expenses families are already facing."The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," he said.WPTV previously spoke with Perez, a handyman whose mobile home is about 250 feet from where the Learjet crashed. At the time, he couldn't access his home, vehicle or the tools he depends on for work. Perez is not one of the residents represented by Garcia, but when WPTV recently returned to the neighborhood, our crew found an orange notice on his mobile home that read "UNSAFE.""Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez told WPTV at the time.He worried then about what the disruption would mean financially."We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made," Perez said.Other organizations have also stepped in to address those immediate needs. The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched a fund offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash. Other groups have provided food, shelter, supplies and services for displaced residents.But some of what these families experienced is more difficult to measure."The photos and the aerials really don't do justice to just how close these families came to being seriously hurt or killed," Garcia said.He said some of the people he's spoken with are still dealing with the emotional and psychological effects of what they experienced."It's not something you see every day, and so it definitely had an emotional or psychological impact on them," Garcia said. "Many of them are having trouble sleeping, which is a very common report when someone undergoes a very sudden, tragic and unexpected event."Garcia, who has practiced law for 32 years, is also a longtime pilot. He described himself as a commercial multi-engine instrument-rated pilot and said he previously co-owned a flight school and charter service out of Palm Beach International Airport.He said determining the impact of emotional trauma will take time."There's no formula for that, Joel. It really depends upon the degree. We rely on medical experts to make that assessment and then use our judgment based on experience," Garcia said.While representing families impacted on the ground, Garcia stressed the magnitude of the loss suffered by the families of those aboard the Learjet."My heart goes out to the victims on board the plane. They suffered a massive loss, and I think what the public needs to understand is that this had a much broader impact," Garcia said.He said his focus now is helping the families he represents move toward some sense of normalcy."It's such a massive loss, particularly to the families of the occupants of the aircraft. It's hard to put words around what those families must be going through," Garcia said. "I can't imagine what they must be going through. And so if I can do something, even just a little bit to help others who were impacted by it, then, you know, I think that's the right thing to do."WPTV has reached out to Aurora Aviation for comment and is working to hear back.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Federal dollars are coming to help local parents continue their college education while dealing with the high cost of childcare.U.S. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., announced Monday a $500,000 annual grant, funded for the next four years, designed to help student parents at Palm Beach State College.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Those accepted into the program based on income guidelines will pay on a sliding scale, anywhere from nothing to $160 a month."Students shouldn’t have to choose between an uplifting career and taking care of their children, and this type of grant gives them the opportunity to do both," Frankel said. Frankel says the average cost of child care in Palm Beach County is around $13,000 annually. The plan is to get 75 parents initially enrolled. Palm Beach State College President Ava Parker says 75% of the students on campus attend college part-time and need to work, so this assistance will allow the parents to find a childcare center close to their home.

Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

Home Schools InnovatED Phase 2 town hall set for Monday at Sebastian River Middle by Tina Hodges Nov 15, 2026 / 12:23 PM A A A A Reset InnovatED (School District of IRC) Share on Twitter Share via Email SEBASTIAN — The School District of Indian River County will hold an InnovatED Phase 2 town hall Monday, November 16, from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. at Sebastian River Middle School to gather public feedback on two facility proposals still under consideration. District officials have invited families, staff, and community members to hear details, ask questions, and share thoughts on the plans. The two proposals focus on a future home for Wabasso School that would add capacity and specialized learning spaces, and on creating a connected arts pathway in Sebastian. Both remain under review, with School Board consideration expected in December. Wabasso School currently serves students with specialized needs on U.S. District leaders have previously described the campus as at capacity and have discussed relocating the program to the former Glendale Elementary site in Vero Beach to allow room for growth and more tailored spaces for life skills and independent learning. The arts pathway proposal involves Sebastian Elementary School of the Arts, which officials have said could share the Sebastian River Middle School campus as a separate school while maintaining its own identity. This is the latest in a series of InnovatED community sessions. Phase 1 of the initiative, which included several school relocations, shared campuses, and boundary adjustments, took effect for the 2026-27 school year after School Board approval in December 2025. The original Sebastian River Middle School town hall for Phase 2 was postponed from Nov. Residents who cannot attend can still submit questions or comments. Share input with the planning team. Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday as the district prepares for the potential for severe weather and heavy rainfall.The district announced that schools will follow a two-hour early release schedule on Tuesday, Nov. 17.The decision comes with current forecasts calling for more rain Tuesday, with heavier rainfall possible into the evening.School officials are asking parents and guardians to consider conditions in their own neighborhoods and along their children's routes to and from school because weather conditions could vary significantly across St. Lucie County.The district said weather-related student absences will be excused.Additional impacts could be possible later in the week. Current forecasts indicate heavier rainfall could continue Wednesday through Friday, potentially causing additional flooding.The district said no decisions have been made about school closures for the remainder of the week.St. Lucie Public Schools said it is working with the Emergency Operations Center and National Weather Service to monitor forecasts, flooding, road conditions and other local impacts.A decision about Tuesday's after-school activities and athletics will be based on weather conditions, with additional information to be released as it becomes available.Families are encouraged to monitor official St. Lucie Public Schools communications for updates.

Trump International Airport continued to face flight cancellations and delays Saturday, a day after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel across the country.WATCH: Travelers Stranded as FAA Ground Stop Fallout ContinuesThe FAA's air traffic control system was back at full operations Saturday, but federal officials warned that delays and cancellations would continue as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said airlines expected to return to full schedules by the end of Sunday. The disruption remained significant Saturday. FlightAware reported more than 6,000 U.S. flight cancellations and over 7,000 delays as of Saturday evening. For some South Florida travelers, those numbers translated into hours spent bouncing between airports and transportation options in hopes of simply getting home.Veterans Karen Matthews and Ron Matthews told WPTV they had been traveling for about 10 hours after their flight from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport to Baltimore was canceled."Are we ever gonna get home?" Karen Matthews said.Their attempt to find another flight brought them from Fort Lauderdale to Donald J. Trump International Airport, but another cancellation awaited them."To have taken the shuttle bus, the train, the shuttle bus ... and then to get here and it's canceled again," Karen Matthews said.She summed up the experience simply: "This is really frustrating."Ron Matthews said the couple had not had a chance to eat during their lengthy trip."It's been kind of rough," he said. "I've been eating mints all day long just to get by."Ron Matthews said American Airlines reissued their tickets but did not provide them with meals, transportation assistance or other accommodations."No accommodations, just reissuing the tickets," he said. "Nothing, no assistance with transportation, no upgrade of seats or anything, not a thing."For Karen Matthews, reaching home also carried a medical concern. She said she needed to get back to medications she takes for blood pressure and acid reflux."I have to control my blood pressure," she said. "So yes, it's important."The nationwide ground stop began Friday afternoon after a telecommunications failure involving air traffic control infrastructure, federal officials said. The stoppage was lifted shortly after 8 p.m. Friday.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a preliminary investigation found the problem occurred while a contractor at a remote FAA facility was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber and working with a router. Officials were still determining whether human error or faulty equipment was responsible.The FAA said airspace was safe and operational Saturday, but airlines still faced the complicated task of getting airplanes, pilots and flight attendants back into position after the nationwide disruption.Another traveler WPTV spoke with, Andrew, said his cancellation came nearly a day after the nationwide disruption."A cancellation the following day, you know, almost 24 hours later, a little bit unexpected," he said.Federal officials said they expected the remaining disruptions to ease through Sunday as airlines rebuilt their schedules. Travelers with upcoming flights should continue checking directly with their airline for the latest status before heading to the airport. For passengers like the Matthews, the nationwide ground stop ending did not mean the travel nightmare was over.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans.Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend."Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. "Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better."For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years."The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years," Sarah Naylor said. "We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember."For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft."I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly," Wyatt said."I like seeing the C-17," Ivy added.The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served."You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes," John Gefell said. Thousands of people dressed in red filled downtown West Palm Beach for this year’s American Heart Association Heart Walk, taking steps to support a cause that touches many families across the community.About 3,000 people took part in the event, which brings together survivors, families and supporters to raise awareness about heart disease and stroke.WATCH: 3,000 walkers fill downtown West Palm Beach for Heart WalkWPTV is a proud sponsor of the Heart Walk, and WPTV’s Ashley Glass served as emcee for this year’s event.For some of the families walking, the mission is deeply personal.WPTV’s Christy Waite has been connecting with the family of a young girl named Blake, whose health journey has included heart failure and multiple open-heart surgeries.Before Blake was born, her parents learned she had a heart condition that would lead to multiple heart surgeries. When Blake was just 14 months old, she became very sick."She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, and that put her heart into heart failure, so she had to have open-heart surgery as soon as possible," her mom, Devin Aubrey, said.Unfortunately, the surgery didn't work, and a few months later Blake had her second open-heart surgery. Doctors put in a mechanical valve to help her heart open and close.As Blake continues to grow, so does her heart, but not the valve. When she is a little older, she will need to have another surgery to fix it.Blake's family formed Team Blake to give back and raise money through the Heart Walk.This year, Team Blake raised $10,000, surpassing the amount the team raised last year.Team Blake wasn’t the only one celebrating a fundraising milestone.This year’s Heart Walk raised more than $1.4 million, setting a new fundraising record.For the walkers who filled downtown West Palm Beach, each step represented a different story, from survivors celebrating how far they’ve come to families walking in support of someone they love.

Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort.Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems.Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach familiesBefore-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water.Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. You first have to empty the houses," French said. "We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out."French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work."People have been just coming and just hands-on," French said. "People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. It’s pretty amazing."Residents seek answers about flooding and drainageAs cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding.Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood.Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process."There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said.Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).Families look for financial assistanceFor some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty.French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available."We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get."Community calls for more volunteersResidents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again.Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance.For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together."To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said.With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent."We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. At 22 games played, the Florida Panthers are a quarter of the way through their regular season.The Panthers have 27 points, tied with Boston for the first Eastern Conference wild card spot.WATCH: Florida Panthers are one-fourth done with their season. Where do they stand?The Panthers are currently playing without Captain Alexander Barkov and Brad Marchand.After a 2-1 overtime loss to the Dallas Stars Sunday night, here’s what Matthew Tkachuk said about the team’s performance so far this season.“Fine, you know, it's been OK, some good and some bad, but we're in the fight. Playing sports can get expensive, especially when you have to pay for all the gear. But one high school student is finding a creative way to combine her favorite sport and giving back. Ella Axtell is a senior at The Benjamin School and founded "Gear for Goals."WATCH: High school senior scores big by giving soccer gear to kids in need"Gear for Goals is an organization that I go and take used and new soccer gear and equipment, and I take it to kids who are less fortunate," Axtell said.Axtell donates the soccer gear to centers like Place of Hope, Family First and Quantum House."They come in there using their wheelchairs. We play soccer with them in any way that they are. We equip them, and it's crazy, they love it so much. They always say how it's able to give them a place to play and give them an advantage to play," Axtell said.She also hosts clinics to teach kids how to play."I love it. I honestly love it because I really do think every kid should have the chance to play, and I don't want one kid not to be able to if they don't have the gear," Axtell said.Gear for Goals is not only helping young athletes in Palm Beach County, but across the world."We've gone all over. I went to Costa Rica internationally with St. Mark's and I held four days in that week. I held soccer clinics and each kid got a full entire kit from shirts to cleats," Axtell said.Axtell said when she came up with the idea for “Gear for Goals”, she started posting online.“We have an Instagram called @Gear_for_goals, and I send out flyers and post all the time about it. And then I started reaching out to other places that I could have boxes at. So I had one at Palm Beach Gardens Rec Center,” Axtell said. “I actually was able to host a soccer drive for dressing for charity at St. Mark's, and we raised money, and got a bunch of money for that. And I just spread the word, have an Amazon wish list. I'm just emailing, emailing, emailing.”Donations have flooded in, with people giving new and slightly used soccer gear or buying from her online equipment wishlist."I just want to continue it. I want to continue it through college. I want to keep going, see how big we can grow and hopefully one day we'll be so big that we'll have clinics all over the world," Axtell said.While helping kids score goals, Axtell says her goal is to grow the organization. She says they're always looking for donations and volunteers. To donate or learn more, visit the @Gear_for_Goals Instagram page.

The Indianapolis Colts got the respite they needed.After losing five straight and enduring three weeks of tumult, they finally celebrated a victory.Daniel Jones threw for one score, Seth McGowan ran for another and Adetomiwa Adebawore recovered a fumble for a touchdown on Sunday as the Colts held on for a 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins to end their skid."It definitely feels good to win," Jones said. "It's hard to win in the NFL, so you have to enjoy them."Colts fans didn't seem to enjoy this one much.Some showed up wearing bags over their heads after Indy shipped away two Pro Bowl captains and their top two receivers before the trade deadline. The Colts held onto Jones and star running back Jonathan Taylor, who said goodbye to Indy fans last week only to suit up again and finish with 103 total yards.While he helped the Colts (3-7) rush for 172 yards, Jones was booed loudly during the second half, when he had just one completion beyond the line of scrimmage. Jones was 11 of 22 for 108 yards with two interceptions.Indy was also flagged 13 times, several of which prevented the Colts from sealing the victory sooner. They wound up needing a fourth-down stop with 1:36 left and McGowan's run for a first down on the ensuing possession to close it out.The offense's struggles led to questions about a possible quarterback switch, which coach Shane Steichen quickly shut down because Indy plays Thursday night."Yeah, he'll be the starting quarterback this week," Steichen said of Jones. "I think we need to continue to get better. There are a lot of things that happen out there every day, self-inflicted wounds for sure, but we've all got to be better."Kyle McCord had a solid starting debut for Miami (1-8), which lost its third straight. He was 17 of 32 for 209 yards, ran for a score and lost one fumble in place of Malik Willis, who went on injured reserve earlier this week with a groin injury. Ollie Gordon II had 20 carries for 76 yards.Miami missed three kicks, including a 51-yard field goal attempt in the fourth quarter that would have given the Dolphins the lead."We've got to make the extra point, and we've got to make the field goal," coach Jeff Hafley said. "It's 24-22, we miss an extra point, which forces us to go for 2, and we miss two field goals, that's seven points. We have to make those."Indy broke a 7-7 tie when Jones found Laquon Treadwell for a 7-yard TD with 39 seconds left in the first half. It was Treadwell's first TD catch since 2021 with Jacksonville.The Colts then swung the game on the Dolphins' first play of the second half when cornerback Justin Walley stripped McCord near the Miami goal line and Adebawore fell on the ball in the end zone to make it 21-7.Zane Gonzalez made a 53-yard field goal to cut the Dolphins' deficit to 21-10, and Miami got within 21-16 on Chris Johnson's 59-yard interception return for a TD — ending the Dolphins' 46-game stretch without a pick-6 that dated to 2023.Shane Spencer extended Indy's margin to 24-16 with a 51-yard field goal, and McCord scored on a 3-yard run before his 2-point conversion pass was broken up by A.J. Haulcy to keep the Colts ahead by two.Dolphins: Miami played without C Aaron Brewer (concussion protocol) and lost DT Zeek Biggers (knee) in the first half. Backup C Andrew Meyer left late in the game with a stinger but returned.Colts: Indy's offensive line already was short-handed without RT Jalen Travis (knee) and it got thinner when LT Bernhard Raimann entered the concussion protocol in the first quarter. The Colts' bigger concern may be the secondary, which lost All-Pro CB Sauce Gardner (calf) and Pro Bowl CB Charvarius Ward (leg) in the third quarter.Gonzalez was wide left on field goal tries from 47 and 51 yards, and the second would have given the Dolphins the lead. He also missed the extra point after the interception return. Gonzalez was promoted from the practice squad Friday after making 5 of 7 field goals and all five of his extra point attempts over the previous three games.Taylor nearly became the fifth Colts player to reach 10,000 yards from scrimmage. He needed 104 yards to join Hall of Famers Marvin Harrison, Edgerrin James and Lenny Moore and current receivers coach Reggie Wayne. But he finished with 16 carries for 83 yards and two catches for 20 yards, leaving him with 9,999.Dolphins: At Buffalo next Sunday.Colts: Go for a season sweep when they visit Houston on Thursday.

Boca Helping Hands is asking the community to help provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families through its annual Thanksgiving Box Brigade.The nonprofit is asking donors to contribute $29.72, the cost of a Thanksgiving box that helps provide families facing food insecurity with the ingredients for a holiday meal.WATCH REPORT BELOW: For families already stretching household budgets, Boca Helping Hands CEO Dr. Andrew Hagen said the added cost of Thanksgiving can make the holiday particularly difficult."You know this has been a tough year for a lot of people economically, and we want to make sure they have a good Thanksgiving," Hagen said.Boca Helping Hands plans to distribute turkeys and Thanksgiving meal boxes to current Pantry Bag Program clients Nov. 21 and 22 at five drive-thru locations in East Boca Raton, West Boca Raton, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach and Lake Worth Beach.Volunteers pack thousands of Thanksgiving boxesPreparing thousands of Thanksgiving meals requires plenty of hands.Volunteers gathered at the Boca Helping Hands food center in Boca Raton to pack the boxes, including a group from Vivmark Residential.Hagen credited the volunteers and community supporters with making the effort possible."We're going to be able to provide at least 4,000 families with Thanksgiving meals, and that's because of the people here today, thanks to you and thanks to all the people that support Boca Helping Hands," Hagen said.To demonstrate the work that goes into the effort, volunteers from Vivmark Residential and The Boca Raton (who donated 100 turkeys) turned packing into a friendly competition. He topped pumpkin pie with meringue and gave it a toasted finish.And when it came to the stuffing, he offered a simple Thanksgiving philosophy."Everything's better with butter," Roenbeck said.The demonstration offered a look at what the ingredients packed by volunteers can ultimately become: a Thanksgiving meal served around a family’s table.How to help Boca Helping HandsCommunity members can support the Thanksgiving Box Brigade by donating the $29.72 cost of a box through Boca Helping Hands.The campaign comes as the nonprofit prepares to serve more than 4,000 families across Palm Beach County for Thanksgiving, turning individual donations and hours of volunteer work into meals families can prepare and share at home.Click here for more information about the Thanksgiving Box Brigade.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer."It's butter."And not just a little butter.During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket.For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey."Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?" Lewis joked. "Those two words do not go together."According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird.Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin.Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter.Lots of butter."You just want to keep working it in there," Lewis said. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code."As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve.After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning.One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird.Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature.Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as:Kosher saltFreshly ground black pepperThymeRosemarySageMix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter.Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey.By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks.Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor.Allow butter to come to room temperature.Mix the butter with kosher salt, black pepper, thyme, rosemary, sage or your favorite herbs.Gently separate the skin from the breast meat without tearing it.Spread seasoned butter beneath the skin and continue working it throughout the breast area.Coat the exterior of the turkey with additional butter.Add additional herbs and seasoning as desired.Place about a half-inch to one inch of water, chicken stock or turkey stock in the bottom of the pan.Cover the turkey with foil and roast at approximately 325 degrees.About 30 minutes before the turkey is done, remove the foil and increase the heat.Lewis says this final step helps create the deep golden-brown color that makes a Thanksgiving turkey look picture-perfect.Of course, Lewis' demonstration included a healthy helping of humor.At one point, while explaining his butter-heavy technique, he declared there is no such thing as too much butter.When told that Thanksgiving calories don't count, he quickly fired back:"What's calories?"And when asked whether anything should go inside the turkey cavity itself, his answer was immediate."Well, butter, of course."For families looking to spend less time in the kitchen and more time around the dinner table, Okeechobee Prime Meat Market is offering a variety of Thanksgiving meal packages featuring roasted or smoked turkeys, prime rib, beef tenderloin, traditional sides and holiday desserts.The market's Ultimate Holiday Family Feast serves 16 to 18 people and includes a Bell & Evans all-natural turkey, prime roasted beef tenderloin, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce and more.Pre-orders are available through Okeechobee Prime Meat Market in West Palm Beach.This article was drafted with the assistance of Microsoft Copilot using reporting, interview transcripts, and information gathered by WPTV journalist T.A. Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony.WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service "It's all like my whole history. Palm Beach County residents can take one Thanksgiving task off their list while helping feed a neighbor in need through Pie It Forward, a fundraiser benefiting Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches.Meals on Wheels Special Events Director Maura Sartory said local chefs from restaurants and country clubs donate pies that are sold through the campaign. Proceeds from each pie sold help feed a senior for one week.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "We sell them online now through Nov. 18, and each pie we sell is available for pickup that Tuesday of Thanksgiving week," Sartory said. "You get a pie and the proceeds feed a senior for a week."The campaign includes traditional Thanksgiving favorites such as pumpkin, pecan and apple pies, along with key lime pies.Orders are available through Nov. 18, although organizers say pies can sell out before the deadline.A pie without the piePeople who will be traveling for Thanksgiving or simply don't need another dessert can still participate.Sartory said Pie It Forward offers a virtual pie, which allows people to make a donation without receiving a physical pie."A lot of people travel during the holidays, so they can still support," Sartory said. "We have a way they can buy a virtual pie, which is simply a donation. A 14-year-old boy was flown to St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach after being injured in an illegal e-bike crash at U.S. 1 and NW Goldenrod Road in Jensen Beach over the weekend, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek expressed frustration over the incident and emphasized the risks associated with illegal e-bikes. “We’re not trying to pick on people, but there’s nothing worse than having a child laid up in a trauma center as we go into the holidays,” Budensiek said. The sheriff’s office released footage of the crash, showing two e-bikes attempting to cross U.S. While the first bike crossed safely, the second rider was struck by a vehicle that had a green light. Budensiek highlighted the importance of helmet use in preventing fatalities. “Had he not been wearing a helmet, we’d be talking about a 14-year-old dying in a fatality crash,” Budensiek said. Earlier this year, the sheriff’s office adopted a zero-tolerance policy on illegal e-bike use to address reckless riding and growing safety concerns. However, Budensiek said the message has not been effective. “So, this is serious for us. I know it’s fun for the kids, but our softer approach has not been working. We’ve had 41 e-bike crashes in Martin County this last year,” Budensiek said. Jason Moore, associate trauma medical director at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, said his hospital has treated numerous patients injured in e-bike crashes. “Yes, unfortunately we’ve seen a lot of e-bike accident patients. I’d say over the last 12 months we’ve seen hundreds of e-bike accidents,” Moore said. Moore described the severity of injuries resulting from e-bike crashes. “Unfortunately, we’ve seen pretty significant injuries, involving brain injuries, broken bones including those in the neck, the collarbone, the ribs. We see quite a few rib fractures,” Moore said. Budensiek said his office is committed to raising awareness about the dangers of illegal e-bikes and is exploring whether parents who knowingly purchase illegal e-bikes for their children could face criminal prosecution. “Parents are knowingly buying illegal e-bikes, giving them to their kids, and allowing their kids to ride them, so we are looking at criminal prosecution for parents if we can make that stick,” Budensiek said. As residents in Jensen Beach continue cleaning up after this month’s historic flooding, another round of heavy rainfall is heading their way. Many of the homes on Hyline Drive were flooded for eight long days, and residents are finally starting to get inside to start cleaning up. Related: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes They’re hoping the rain doesn’t ruin their progress. “Eight days of standing water. There was nothing that we could do but watch everything deteriorate and mold,” Susan Destafney said. Destafney’s home sits next to the Hyline Pond and was filled with dirty floodwater for eight days. She said they lost almost everything, and now volunteers are tearing the home down to the studs and treating it for mold. “I've cried more than I've ever cried before. It's just a lot to take in, and it should never have happened,” Destafney said. County officials have pumped water from the neighborhood and the pond, and they have set up a recovery assistance webpage for residents. But Destafney said for their day-to-day needs, they are relying on the volunteers and nonprofits to help them get by. She worries they could be knocked back to square one if the forecasted rainfall this week causes more flooding. I mean, things that I was able to save, I do have on my back porch. So, it's going to be raining. So, what's going to happen to the few things that I was able to save? It's a lot,” Destafney said. Others in the community we spoke to are also concerned about the forecast. We're trying to recover right now. My friends are trying to recover right now. All these efforts for cleanup to get us in a place to where it's dried up, the water is gone, and now they're expecting flash flooding again. So, yeah, we're nervous that this is going to be like what it was a couple of days ago all over again in a few days,” Crystal van Duyme said. WPBF 25 News reached out to the county to see what they’re doing to prep for the upcoming rainfall. The public works director was not available Monday, but we’re hoping to speak with him on Tuesday. However, residents did tell us that crews are currently draining the Hyline Pond again, likely in preparation for that rain. WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said the ranking combines behaviors that can have very different effects. How WalletHub ranked the cities WalletHub compared the 150 most populated U.S. cities and at least two of the most populated cities in each state. Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

The School District of Indian River County will operate on a modified schedule Tuesday as a precaution ahead of expected rain and the potential for heavier rainfall. The district announced the schedule change Monday afternoon for Tuesday, Nov. Under the modified-day schedule, extracurricular activities will conclude by 2:30 p.m. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but will be closed Tuesday afternoon, according to the district. The district said families should make decisions based on the conditions in their area. If weather conditions prevent a student from attending school, the resulting absence will be excused. Rain is expected Tuesday, with heavier rainfall possible Tuesday evening. The district also warned that heavier rainfall could continue Wednesday through Friday. The School District of Indian River County said additional updates will be provided by 1 p.m. the day before any additional schedule changes. Families should continue monitoring official district communications for the latest information.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie faces renewed flood threat with 4 to 6 inches of rain forecast
hero.body:
Another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days in Port St. Lucie, threatening renewed flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from record rainfall two weeks ago. St. Lucie Public Schools announced a two-hour early release Tuesday.

County crews have been inspecting canals and drainage systems, clearing them ahead of the expected rain. Officials warn that the ground remains saturated from recent storms, meaning far less rain than usual could cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. The school district announced the early dismissal to avoid a repeat of the flooding problems that affected students taking buses home earlier this month.

The earlier flooding stranded cars, trapped some families in their homes and forced others to wade through deep water. “It was horrible,” said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. “Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods.” With more heavy rain forecast, Perez said he planned to get supplies before flooding returned.

Freshman Noah Julian was among those caught in the earlier flooding. He stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson spread quickly on social media, showing him swimming through floodwaters to reach his driveway. His father, Romeo Julian, expressed concern about alligators, snakes and sharp objects in the water.

Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and prepare for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

hero.headline: Martin County sheriff weighs e-bike seizures, parent charges after Jensen Beach crash
hero.body:
The Martin County sheriff is considering seizing illegal e-bikes and pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. The sheriff outlined the potential crackdown Monday after a Jensen Beach crash left a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy with catastrophic injuries.

The boy was struck Sunday near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road and was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was in stable condition, the sheriff said at a news conference. He and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes before attempting to cross U.S. 1. The friend made it across, but a northbound vehicle with a green light struck the 14-year-old. The impact threw him approximately 50 feet, and his e-bike landed about 100 feet away.

Investigators determined the boy was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The sheriff described the motorbike-style vehicle as illegal for street use. The boy was wearing a helmet, which the sheriff credited with helping him survive the crash.

The proposed seizures and potential charges against parents would represent tougher consequences following educational workshops, warnings and previous enforcement efforts. The sheriff said those efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Martin County has recorded 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders ranging in age from 7 to 80, according to the sheriff.

The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

cards.headline: Family Night set for Tuesday at Jensen Beach’s Festival of Giving
cards.teaser: More than 50 nonprofits are taking part in the festival at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast. Events continue through Saturday, with an adult holiday pajama party Friday.
cards.body:
Family Night is scheduled for Tuesday evening, Nov. 17, at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast in Jensen Beach as part of the third annual Festival of Giving. More than 50 local nonprofits are participating in the festival, which fills the museum with decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays. The event introduces visitors to organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast and gives those groups an opportunity to share their work. The festival continues through Saturday, Nov. 21, at 2 p.m., according to Christina McIntosh, the museum’s community outreach and events coordinator.

Participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast, McIntosh said. “Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,” she said. The holiday displays serve as introductions to the organizations and the work they do throughout the region.

The gathering also gives participating organizations a chance to learn about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits taking part. “The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,” said Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers. “We get to understand what they do.”

An adult holiday pajama party is scheduled for Friday. “We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed,” McIntosh said. The Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast is at 1707 NE Indian River Drive in Jensen Beach. More information is available at www.childrensmuseumtc.org.

hero.headline: More heavy rain threatens Jensen Beach as Hyline Drive residents clean up after flooding
hero.body:
Another round of heavy rain is forecast this week as Jensen Beach residents begin cleaning up homes on Hyline Drive that were flooded for eight days. Residents worry renewed flooding could undo their progress as volunteers help remove damaged materials and treat homes for mold.

Susan Destafney’s home next to the Hyline Pond was filled with dirty floodwater for eight days. She said she lost almost everything, and volunteers are tearing the home down to the studs and treating it for mold. “Eight days of standing water. There was nothing that we could do but watch everything deteriorate and mold,” Destafney said.

County officials have pumped water from the neighborhood and the pond. They have also established a recovery assistance webpage for residents. Residents said crews are draining the Hyline Pond again as more rainfall approaches. Destafney said she is relying on volunteers and nonprofits for day-to-day needs during the cleanup.

Some belongings Destafney managed to save are on her back porch, leaving her worried about what the coming rain could do to them. She fears another flood could put her back at square one. “I've cried more than I've ever cried before. It's just a lot to take in, and it should never have happened,” she said.

Crystal van Duyme also expressed concern about the forecast as she and her friends work to recover. She said cleanup efforts have focused on getting the area dry after the floodwater receded, and the prospect of flash flooding has residents nervous about a repeat of the conditions they recently endured.

hero.headline: Rio Marine Village breaks ground in Jensen Beach with 342 apartments and marina
hero.body:
Rio Marine Village, a 30-acre mixed-use development in Jensen Beach, broke ground Thursday after more than five years of planning. The Martin County project will include 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina and more than a half-mile of public riverwalk.

Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions.

Plans call for public waterfront access through a riverwalk, park, boardwalk and beach, along with kayak and paddleboard rentals. In addition to waterfront dining and entertainment destinations, the development will feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue.

Among the restaurants will be a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse, owned by football legend Joe Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica. A second outdoor dining concept is also planned.

“The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water,” Namath said. “Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together.”

hero.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools to dismiss two hours early Tuesday ahead of potential severe weather
hero.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday, Nov. 17, ahead of potential severe weather and heavy rainfall. The district announced that schools will follow a two-hour early release schedule as forecasts call for more rain Tuesday, with heavier rainfall possible into the evening. Weather-related student absences will be excused, the district said.

School officials are asking parents and guardians to consider conditions in their neighborhoods and along their children’s routes to and from school. Weather conditions could vary significantly across St. Lucie County. The district said decisions about Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics will be based on weather conditions, and it will release additional information as it becomes available.

Decisions about school closures for the remainder of the week remain pending. Current forecasts indicate heavier rainfall could continue Wednesday through Friday, potentially causing additional flooding and further impacts later in the week.

St. Lucie Public Schools said it is working with the Emergency Operations Center and National Weather Service to monitor forecasts, flooding, road conditions and other local impacts. Families are encouraged to monitor official St. Lucie Public Schools communications for updates.

hero.headline: Vehicles moved off I-95 after crashes near Hobe Sound; congestion lingers
hero.body:
All vehicles have been moved off I-95 after two crashes near Hobe Sound in Martin County on Monday morning, but congestion remains in both directions. One crash blocked the two left southbound lanes beyond Exit 96, while a second crash nearby affected northbound traffic.

One crash involved a single vehicle and the other involved three vehicles, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. No injuries have been reported in either crash.

The southbound crash was reported at about 11:15 a.m. and was still affecting traffic at 11:21 a.m., according to the Florida Department of Transportation’s FL511 traffic system. Drivers can check FL511 for the latest traffic updates.
